newsitem.title: Bulgaria: Bulgarian opposition holds celebration rallies.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian opposition holds celebration rallies.

text.p: Tens of thousands of Bulgarians flocked to emotional celebration rallies on Wednesday after President Petar Stoyanov brokered a deal for early elections.
Some 15,000 students held a victory march to celebrate the success of their month-long protest, stopping outside the presidency in a tribute to Stoyanov, who took office just two weeks ago.

After 30 days of mass rallies fuelled by economic crisis, the Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP) on Tuesday agreed to give up attempts to form another government. Elections are set for April, 20 months ahead of schedule.

The students, accompanied by a band of Gypsy musicians, carried banners reading "Happy and free Bulgaria" and "If the screen reads BSP, just press delete". One student sprayed the crowd with champagne.

Stoyanov came out to greet the students but they demanded a speech. "This is your victory. This victory doesn't mean only elections, it also means that the conscience and the dignity of the Bulgarian nation is still alive, and it is still very sensitive to peoples' suffering," he told them.
The students were joined by a crowd of about 1,000 people from the town of Doupnitsa, south of Sofia, who blocked road and rail links to Greece around the clock for seven days.
The crowd chanted "We love you" and "We are with you". Stoyanov had tears in his eyes as he joined them singing the national anthem.
"Your protests did not stop only with demands for low bread and food prices. You went far beyond that and you restored the dignity and pride of the Bulgarian nation," he said.
"Despite your victory it is my duty to tell you that this is just the beginning, and you should celebrate only after real reforms are implemented in Bulgaria."
More than 30,000 jubilant opposition supporters gathered for a victory rally outside the Alexander Nevsky cathedral, where a special mass was said earlier in the day.
"Never in our history have we been so united and categorical in our demands," Ivan Kostov, leader of the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces, told the crowd.
"We are not the same, we are different people, we know what we want and how to achieve it," said Kostov, opening a bottle of champagne on the speakers' podium.
According to the constitution, Stoyanov must now dissolve parliament and appoint a caretaker cabinet by February 20. Elections are expected on April 13 or 20.
Stoyanov warned jubilant crowds on Tuesday that hard times still lay ahead, and Bulgarians returned on Wednesday to the grim reality of bread and petrol queues.

The International Monetary Fund said it would resume talks on aid to pull Bulgaria back from the brink of default on its $10 billion debt as soon as an interim government was in place, boosting Bulgarian Brady bonds on the secondary debt market.
Central bank foreign exchange reserves fell to $415 million at end-January from $955.6 million a year earlier.

The collapse of the national currency has caused huge losses to the state-owned Neftohim refinery, which lacks the cash to pay suppliers. The outgoing cabinet on Wednesday raised petrol and diesel prices by an average of 48 percent.
Most coal miners went back to work on Wednesday but the Pernik and Bobov Dol mines are still on strike for more pay.
Sofia students plan a cleanup campaign on Thursday to remove the debris from their roadblocks around the capital.
